extracted.intended_audience: general readers, business journalists, and corporate-governance professionals interested in corporate scandals and company disclosures
extracted.subtask_description: Drafting or evaluating press releases and communications about a corporate governance/accounting scandal (using the Olympus affair as background). Useful for summarising events, explaining governance failings, and communicating legal and reputational consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The independence of directors should be adequate; the article criticises that 'the independence of the directors was inadequate' and that 12 out of 15 directors were either executives or former executives of the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards should include a meaningful proportion of independent directors (not current or former executives) to provide effective oversight; avoid boards dominated by insiders. Examples/anti-patterns: a board where most members are executives or ex-executives reduces challenge to management decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditor responsibility and effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditors must detect and properly question irregularities; the piece notes auditors (KPMG and Ernst & Young) 'would have to answer tough questions about why the manipulation was never discovered or properly questioned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External auditors should exercise professional scepticism, probe unusual transactions, and escalate concerns. Indicators of failure include delayed discovery of large 'success fees' or write‑downs and audit sign-offs despite contradictory signals. Pay, workload, or conflicts that impede audit quality (e.g., low fees, overwork) are anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely disclosure of losses and material information
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must disclose losses and material financial information promptly; the article references 'mark to market' rules made mandatory in 1999 obliging timely disclosure of securities investment losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial statements and disclosures should reflect true exposures in a timely manner. Delayed or obscured disclosure (e.g., hiding losses via off‑book schemes) undermines investor confidence and may breach regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence of internal and external evaluation teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquisitions and valuations should be evaluated by competent internal and external teams; the article raises 'uncomfortable questions about the competence of the internal and external teams that evaluated the three acquisitions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due diligence and valuation teams should have relevant expertise and deliver realistic forecasts. Red flags: unrealistic sales forecasts used to justify acquisition prices and dramatic subsequent write-downs (e.g., combined sales targets reduced by 93%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness and transparency of advisory fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Advisory and success fees should be reasonable and disclosed; the article documents an advisory fee of US$687 million (31% of the acquisition price) where typical fees are 1–2%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptionally large or opaque adviser fees require explanation and scrutiny. Press releases and disclosures should explain fee structures and beneficiaries; unexplained outsized fees are an anti-pattern and a potential sign of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board oversight and proper approval of transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: The board must properly oversee and approve significant payments and transactions; commentary states 'the fact that the board approved the payment cannot have been a correct decision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards should ensure approvals follow rigorous review, independent advice, and clear documentation. Rubber‑stamping or approving complex deals without adequate review indicates governance failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of concealment schemes (tobashi) and off‑book manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must not conceal losses using unlawful schemes (e.g., 'Tobashi'); the article describes use of tobashi schemes to hide substantial trading losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent accounting and honest reporting are required; use of off‑book vehicles or contrived transactions to hide losses is unlawful and unethical. Press communications should make clear that concealment practices are unacceptable and explain corrective steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate culture of accountability and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisational culture should prioritise accountability, challenge authority, and transparency; the article cites criticism of a 'culture of denial' and 'a lack of accountability among senior executives; inadequate disclosure; a disinclination to challenge authority and absolute deference to corporate boards.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firms should encourage open challenge, protect whistleblowers, and prioritise long‑term value over short‑term reputation management. Communications should address root cultural causes, not merely apologise for market effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of undue influence from creditors or banks
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate decision‑making and board composition should not be subject to 'undue influence' from creditor banks or other stakeholders whose interests diverge from shareholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board nominations and strategic decisions must balance creditor input and shareholder interests; disclose relationships with major creditors and ensure independence in decision-making. Anti-pattern: promoting ex-bankers who may prioritise banks' interests ahead of shareholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareholder communication that addresses causes, not only effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Public communication should explain causes of problems rather than focusing only on effects like share price movements; critic says an apology that 'trivialises the possible wrongdoings and misplaces emphasis on an effect rather than the cause' is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press statements should transparently explain root causes, remedial actions, and accountability steps. Avoid messaging that downplays wrongdoing by emphasising inconvenience or share‑price impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of special‑purpose vehicles and beneficiary identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of SPVs and offshore entities must be transparent; the article documents 'Seventeen Cayman and BVI special purpose vehicles' and that the identity of the beneficiary (Axam Investments) 'was only made publicly known more than 18 months later.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose the purpose, beneficiaries, and controllers of any SPVs used in transactions. Opaqueness or delayed disclosure of beneficiaries is a red flag for potential asset diversion or concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of advisor identities and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Advisors and their relationships should be disclosed to avoid conflicts; the article notes Perella Weinberg and Weil, Gotshal & Manges were disclosed advisors while Axes/Axam (which received large fees) was not initially transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press materials and filings should list all advisers, consultants, and intermediaries involved in major deals and disclose any prior relationships that could create conflicts. Failure to disclose hidden intermediaries is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement and legal accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be effective legal and regulatory remedies for breaches (criminal charges, fines, civil suits); the article records arrests, fines, suspended sentences, and large shareholder-derivative damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate responses and public statements should acknowledge regulatory findings and cooperate with investigations; credible enforcement (criminal, civil, administrative) is part of deterrence and restoring confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit firm independence and avoidance of auditor shopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditors should be independent and not be switched to avoid scrutiny; the article references Olympus switching auditors after clashes and questions why a Japanese auditor signed off when other network members refused clean opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain auditor independence, rotate auditors appropriately, and avoid changing auditors for the purpose of obtaining more favourable opinions. Transparent rationale must be provided for any auditor changes.
